title: A Galaxy of Birth and Death
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2403, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/M. T. Patterson (New Mexico State University). Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Glowing red spots dot NGC 2403, a spiral galaxy also cataloged as Caldwell 7, in this picture from the Mosaic camera on Kitt Peak's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope. Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO) is part of NSF NOIRLab. The red patches are H II regions, clouds of ionized hydrogen that mark where young, hot stars are being born.

Newborn stars often ionize the hydrogen around them as they form, making it glow. NGC 2403 has also seen the other end of a star's life. It hosted SN 2004dj, described as the brightest and nearest stellar death observed so far this millennium. The part of the galaxy holding the star that exploded in 2004 was observed before, during and after the blast, giving a revealing timeline of the event.

Stars form over timescales far longer than a human lifetime, so astronomers must piece their story together like a puzzle, studying different stars at different stages. Supernovae unfold very quickly, even by human standards, which makes them valuable for testing and refining theories of how stars live and die.

understand.summary: Taken with the Mosaic camera on the NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope through U, B, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color mapping isn't published.
